paragraphs.heading: A game worth infinity, or a few dollars
paragraphs.text: The St. Petersburg paradox is about a coin-tossing game whose expected payoff is infinite. Yet to the people who might play it, the game seems worth only a small sum. It is a warning about a simple decision rule: if you judge choices by expected value alone, the rule can recommend something that presumably no real person would ever do.

paragraphs.heading: How the game works
paragraphs.text: A casino offers one player a game with a fair coin, tossed again and again. The pot starts at 2 dollars and doubles every time the coin shows tails. The first time heads shows, the game is over and the player collects the pot. So heads on the first toss pays 2 dollars, tails then heads pays 4, two tails then heads pays 8, and so on. Written as a formula, the prize is 2ᵏ⁺¹ dollars, where k is the number of tails in a row.

paragraphs.heading: Where the paradox lies
paragraphs.text: The natural question is what price would be fair to pay for a turn. When you add up the expected winnings, the total keeps growing with no limit, so the expected win is infinite. If the only thing you cared about was the expected change in your money, you should accept any entry price at all. The paradox is the gap between that endless value and the modest amount people actually seem ready to pay.

paragraphs.heading: Two Bernoullis
paragraphs.text: Nicolas Bernoulli came up with the problem and set it out in a letter to Pierre Raymond de Montmort dated September 9, 1713. The puzzle is named after the work of his cousin Daniel Bernoulli, who lived for a time in Saint Petersburg. In 1738 Daniel published his analysis in the Commentaries of that city's Imperial Academy of Science.

paragraphs.heading: Money matters less when you have more
paragraphs.text: The classic answer brings in utility: the idea that an item's value should rest on the use it gives you, not on its price. It adds the assumption that extra money brings less and less benefit. A gain of a thousand ducats means more to a pauper than to a rich man, even though the amount is the same. Under this view, what you should pay depends on how wealthy you are. With natural log utility, a millionaire should pay up to $20.88, while someone with $1,000 should pay up to $10.95.

paragraphs.heading: Why that fix is not the end
paragraphs.text: In a letter to Nicolas Bernoulli, another thinker showed that a square root function, standing for the shrinking benefit of gains, could also settle the problem. Unlike Daniel Bernoulli, he looked only at the money won in the lottery, not at a person's total wealth. These utility answers are not fully satisfying, though. Change the game so the prizes grow even faster, and the paradox comes back. Menger was the first to point out that for any utility function without an upper limit, some lottery brings back a version of the paradox.

paragraphs.heading: Other ways out
paragraphs.text: Nicolas Bernoulli had his own idea: people may simply ignore events that are very unlikely. In this game, only unlikely outcomes produce the huge prizes behind the infinite expected value, so ignoring them could remove the paradox. The idea of weighting probabilities came back much later in the prospect theory of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky. Another proposed answer is practical: the game assumes the casino has endless resources, and no casino could hold the impossible sums needed to keep it going forever.
